scenario: AITA for being home all day and refusing to cook for my mom? | I'm a female in my senior year of high school and I have a younger sister in grade 10. As most of you know, schools have been closed for a while now and won't reopen for at least another month. My dad gets to work from home, but my mom still has to go out to her office. My school just started online teaching, and we've been getting a lot of assignments to complete. However, my mom expects us to make dinner basically every night because "we're home all day". That really annoyed me because yeah "we're home all day" but we have school work to do. I got upset and asked her why doesn't she cook, since she always finishes work at 5 pm and her office is like 6 minutes from home. Well, once she got home today and saw there was no dinner prepared, she got pissed and started screaming at me how she's so ashamed of us and how we're useless. When I explained how yes we're home all day but doesn't mean we have the whole day off, she got even more mad and said that it doesn't take that long to cook. I refuted by "why don't you cook then?" For more context, my mom is an awful cook. She literally puts no effort into learning or looking up recipes. My dad is an excellent cook. He's tried to teach her before, but she refuses to learn and complains. Before, he would cook for us almost every day, even if he came home late from work (he has a high demanding job so his hours range but he's home 6 pm the EARLIEST, sometimes as late as 9 or even 10 pm. + 30-40 minutes one way commuting). And what does he come home to? Either a low effort flavourless meal from my mom, or my mom sitting on her ass watching TV and asking him what's he's gonna make for dinner. So my dad is forced to make dinner at a late hour so he can eat. More recently, he would just eat fast-food before coming home because he doesn't expect dinner to be on the table. However, he asks if us girls are hungry and offers to cook something for us to eat because he's worried that our mom didn't make us a proper meal. I'm a good cook too (self taught), and I try to help out if I don't have too much homework to do. I did a lot of the cooking during the first 3 weeks before online school started, as well as baking lots of treats like breads, cookies, meringues etc. Also, my dad does practically all the chores in the house, while my mom spends all her time sitting on her ass watching TV. So AITA for not cooking dinner today and telling my mom to not expect dinner every time she comes home? Also, my dad ended cooking in the end today.

I did a lot of the cooking during the first 3 weeks before online school started, as well as baking lots of treats like breads, cookies, meringues etc. Also, my dad does practically all the chores in the house, while my mom spends all her time sitting on her ass watching TV. So AITA for not cooking dinner today and telling my mom to not expect dinner every time she comes home? Also, my dad ended cooking in the end today.

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: 0 (Not the asshole) ### Why: - **Your schoolwork is legitimate and demanding**: Online classes, assignments, and exams require focus and time—especially as a high school senior. "Home all day" does **not** mean "available for full-time domestic labor." Schools are not "free time"; they’re structured academic obligations. - **Your mom’s expectations are unreasonable**: She works only 6 minutes from home and returns by 5 PM, yet expects *you* (a student) to cook dinner *every night* while she watches TV. Meanwhile, she refuses to learn to cook herself (even though your dad has tried to teach her), and her meals are "low effort" or "flavorless." Her behavior is lazy and unfair. - **Your dad is already shouldering the burden**: He works long hours, commutes, and often eats fast food before home because he knows dinner won’t be ready. Yet he still steps in to cook for you when needed. This highlights the *real* issue: **your mom is avoiding responsibility**, and your dad is compensating for her. - **You’ve already contributed**: You cooked during the first 3 weeks and bake treats when homework allows. This shows willingness to help—but you’re not obligated to be the primary cook *every single night* while balancing school. - **Your mom’s reaction is disproportionate**: Calling you "useless" or "ashamed" for refusing to cook while she does nothing is emotional manipulation. She’s shifting blame onto you instead of taking accountability for her own role in the household. ### The real problem: Your mom is using "we’re home all day" as an excuse to avoid work she’s capable of doing (e.g., learning to cook, cleaning, or planning meals), while expecting you to fill the gap. This is **unfair and unsustainable**. Healthy households share responsibilities *proportionally*: - A working parent shouldn’t demand kids cook *every night* while they relax. - A parent who refuses to improve basic skills (like cooking) shouldn’t blame others for their own shortcomings. - Your dad’s actions prove he recognizes this imbalance—he’s cooking for you because *he* knows it’s unfair to expect you to do it all. ### What you should do: - **Talk to your dad**: Explain the situation clearly. He’s the adult who can advocate for fairness (e.g., "Mom should cook or we should split chores evenly"). - **Set boundaries**: "I’ll help cook 2–3 nights a week when my homework allows, but I can’t do it every night. Mom needs to step up too." - **Document chores**: If your mom continues to dismiss your efforts, write down who does what (e.g., "Mom: 0 chores, Dad: 90% cooking/cleaning, Me: 10% cooking when possible"). This makes the imbalance obvious. **You are not the asshole**—you’re a student doing your best to balance school and family. The real issue is your mom’s lack of contribution and refusal to take accountability. This isn’t about "refusing to help"; it’s about refusing to be exploited as free labor while she does nothing. 🌟
